payload.title: The Return of the Night Train
paragraphs: For thirty years the sleeper train looked like a museum piece. Budget airlines undercut it, new high-speed lines made daytime journeys short enough to finish before dinner, and one European operator after another sold off its carriages. Then, towards the end of the last decade, bookings began to climb again. Austrian, Swedish and Dutch companies bought rolling stock that had been standing unused in sidings, and routes closed for years reopened between capitals a thousand kilometres apart.

The usual explanation is climate. A night train produces a small fraction of the carbon dioxide of the equivalent flight, and in several countries flying has acquired a faint sense of embarrassment. Yet the operators are careful not to build a business on guilt alone. What sells the tickets, their own surveys suggest, is time: a passenger who boards at ten in the evening and steps out in the centre of another city at breakfast has spent none of their waking hours travelling, and has paid for no hotel.

The economics remain awkward. A sleeper carries far fewer paying passengers than a seated train of the same length, it occupies expensive track at night when maintenance crews would rather have it, and it has to be cleaned and staffed like a small hotel. Governments that want the service therefore tend to pay for it, either directly or by lending money for new carriages. Whether that support survives the first bad year is the question the operators, privately, are still asking.

Governments have discovered that night trains earn more money per passenger than any other kind of rail service.

payload.title: Four Days, Five Days' Pay
paragraphs: A few years ago sixty-one British companies agreed to try something their competitors thought reckless: five days of pay for four days of work, with no fall in what the staff were expected to produce. The firms ranged from a fish-and-chip shop to a software house with several hundred employees. Researchers tracked revenue, sick days and staff turnover for six months, and when the trial ended fifty-six of the sixty-one chose to carry on.

The findings are easy to overstate. Revenue held steady rather than rising sharply, and the companies that volunteered were, almost by definition, ones already confident that their work could be reorganised. What changed most was not output but the shape of the week. Meetings were cut, some of them by half, and long stretches of uninterrupted work replaced the habit of being visibly available. Employees reported sleeping better; managers reported spending less time chasing people for updates.

Where the model struggles is in work that cannot be compressed. A hospital ward, a bus route or a shop counter needs someone standing in it for a fixed number of hours, so a shorter week there means hiring more people rather than working differently. Several trials in such places have quietly ended. The lesson may be that the four-day week is less a universal reform than a test of how much of an ordinary office week was ever really work.

Hospitals and bus companies have found the four-day week easier to introduce than software firms have.
